paras: The lynching of J. L. Jennings was the hanging of Jennings, a farm hand accused of murder, after an armed band took him from the jail at Tierra Amarilla, the seat of Rio Arriba County, New Mexico Territory, on the night of July 23 or 24, 1881. Jennings had been arrested with Mrs. Lewis, the wife of his employer, after the body of the farmer Lewis was found buried near an irrigation ditch on the Animas River, and both were reported to have confessed. A two-line Santa Fe brief ran from California to Maine, and fuller accounts blamed a vigilance committee that thought the jail unsafe.

According to Canon City and Santa Fe reports, the Lewis family, a husband, wife and three children, moved from Canon City, Colorado, to the upper Animas River near Farmington with Jennings as their hired man. Lewis disappeared in early July; the Santa Fe dispatch of July 28 gave July 4, while the Associated Press report from Santa Fe and a letter from a neighbor gave the 8th. Searchers found his body buried beside an irrigation ditch, and the reports said Jennings had killed him at Mrs. Lewis's instigation so that the two could marry.

A crowd gathered at the grave with a rope, and Jennings confessed on a promise of protection. Justice of the Peace Haines and the sheriff, given as Blanchett, Blancott or Blanchard, were credited with preventing a lynching, and according to the Durango Southwest the sheriff told the crowd "that Judge Lynch Itad ceased to hold forth."

After an examination before the justice, Jennings was committed to await the grand jury and taken under guard to the county jail at Tierra Amarilla. The Santa Fe dispatch of July 28 said people deemed the county jail unsafe because two Mexicans charged with murder had recently escaped from it, and that "the Vigilance Committee took the matter in hand." An Associated Press and Denver Tribune dispatch dated Santa Fe, July 26, said a band of armed men rode to the jail on Saturday night, overpowered the jailer, took Jennings out and hanged him to a tree. The Wheeling version added that the band held a court "presided over by Judge Lynch" before the hanging. Mrs. Lewis, held in an adjoining cell, was not harmed, and her trial was reported set for September.
A brief carried by the Mower County Transcript gave the lynchers as "a party of forty citizens"; no report names any of them or states the race of anyone involved.

Later summaries said Mrs. Lewis was still in jail, held for complicity, and that the three children were left without a home, though the Wheeling dispatch said the community was caring for them. No report of an inquest into Jennings's death or of arrests of the lynchers appears in the coverage.

Most papers knew the case only from the Denver Republican's two-line Santa Fe special, which called Jennings a man "who recently murdered a man" and said he was lynched on Sunday. Editors headed it "Murderer Lynched," "Lynching of a Murderer," "Lynched in New Mexico" and "Judge Lynch Administers Justice." Through August the item circulated in weekly news-summary columns in New Hampshire, New Jersey, Wisconsin, Minnesota, Missouri, Tennessee, Rhode Island and South Carolina.

Fuller accounts treated the hanging as a regional custom: the Wheeling Daily Intelligencer subtitled its story "The Western Way of Dealing with Prisoners at Insecure Jails." In the territory, the Santa Fe New Mexican, quoted by the Las Vegas Daily Gazette, said the temptation to "mete out summary justice" to the author of a "sickening murder" had been "too great to be resisted," and added that Jennings deserved his punishment, though it regretted he had not died by the decree of the law.

The date of the lynching differs: the Republican special said Sunday, July 24, while the July 26 Associated Press dispatch and the July 28 Santa Fe dispatch said Saturday night, July 23, and the Omaha Bee's version of the July 28 dispatch said "to-day," which conflicts with the earlier dispatches. Reports also differ on whether Jennings had been in jail "some two weeks" or only one night.

accounts.label: AP / Denver Tribune dispatch, Santa Fe Jul 26
accounts.gist: Because the jail was unsafe, a band of armed men rode to it on Saturday night, overpowered the jailer and hanged Jennings to a tree; Mrs. Lewis was not molested.

accounts.label: Santa Fe dispatch, Jul 28
accounts.gist: A Vigilance Committee's armed band took Jennings out 'on Saturday last', held a court under 'Judge Lynch', found him guilty and hanged him to a tree.

accounts.label: Santa Fe New Mexican
accounts.gist: Jennings was lynched the first night after he was brought from Farmington to the county seat; he deserved it, though a legal death would have been better.

accounts.label: Western news brief
accounts.gist: A party of forty citizens lynched 'H. T. Jennings' for murdering Abe Lewis to possess his wife.

framing.detail: The Republican special ran under 'Murderer Lynched', 'Lynching of a Murderer', 'Lynched in New Mexico', presenting Jennings's guilt as fact.
Wheeling's 'The Western Way of Dealing with Prisoners at Insecure Jails' explained the lynching by the unsafe jail without comment.
The Santa Fe New Mexican said Jennings deserved the mob's punishment, regretting only that the law had not done it.
The Canon City paper centered the murdered man and his children and reported the lynching through dispatches.

conflicts.note: The Saturday accounts are the fuller and independent dispatches; the Omaha 'to-day' conflicts with dispatches of Jul 26.
